caption:
"Are refusals going up?" It is the question we get every time a headline runs.

Refusal rates move, and they vary considerably by consulate and by nationality. But almost every refusal we review comes down to the same thing: the file, not the person.

Incomplete documents. Dates that do not match. A financial story with a gap in it. Those are fixable.

slides.headline: "ARE REFUSALS GOING UP?"
slides.sub: Asked every time a headline runs.
slides.note: Rates move, and they differ sharply by consulate and nationality. The more useful question is why files fail.

slides.answer: ALMOST ALWAYS, IT IS THE FILE.
slides.body: Not the person. Not the passport. The overwhelming majority of refusals we review trace back to documents that did not hold together.
slides.note: Which is genuinely good news, because that part is fixable.

slides.headline: WHAT WE SEE MOST
items: Documents that contradict each other on dates or amounts
A sudden deposit with no visible history
Reservations that do not match the stated itinerary
No evidence of what the applicant returns to
The wrong consulate for the actual trip

slides.headline: HOW PEOPLE READ THE NEWS
slides.never: Conclude that approval is now a lottery and submit a weaker file because it probably will not matter. It matters more when scrutiny rises, not less.
slides.instead: Assume the file will be read carefully, and build one that survives being read carefully. That is the entire strategy.

slides.headline: WE AUDIT BEFORE THEY DO.
slides.sub: Better we find it than they do.

slides.headline: SEND ONE MESSAGE. WE DO THE REST.
